transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Lee. It's real nice to meet you. Um, is it okay if I sit here? 

Well, I guess I'm here because... I really don't want to sound like I'm just complaining or causing trouble for my family, I always try to keep the peace. But it's just this situation with my husband's sister. She’s... well, she's been working this family business in a way where she can get control of the money and, you know, push me out of making any decisions. 

I know it probably sounds silly to bring up, and folks keep trying to smooth it over and make it seem like it's nothing, but... well, I know what I’ve been seeing for more than a year now. I'm sorry to just dump all that on you right away. Am I explaining that okay?

Aside from this situation with your husband's sister, do you often find yourself feeling that other people—friends, coworkers, or other family members—are trying to take advantage of you or can't be trusted?

Oh, goodness, no. No, not at all. I hope I didn't make it sound like I'm just... you know, a suspicious person or always looking for trouble. I really try to see the good in everybody, I truly do. 

My friends are wonderful, and the rest of the family is just lovely. We all get along real well. I don't have any problems trusting folks normally. It's really just... just this one specific thing with his sister. That's why it's so hard for me to even bring it up, because I'm not the type to point fingers or stir the pot with people. 

Is that helpful? I just want to make sure I'm answering your questions right.

If your family showed you clear evidence that your husband's sister wasn't trying to take control of the money or push you out of decisions, do you think that could change your mind, or does what you've seen feel certain to you no matter what?

Oh... well, I know they mean well, I really do. And I'd never want to be stubborn or, you know, difficult about it. I always try to listen to what my family says. 

But... I mean, I've just seen it with my own eyes, you know? For over a year now, the way she handles the accounts, the little things she does to keep me out of the loop... it's just so clear to me. I know they try to smooth it over because nobody likes conflict, and I hate conflict too, I really do. But no matter what they say or what they show me, I just... I know what I know. I can't just pretend I haven't seen her trying to take over the money and push me out. 

Does that make me sound awful? I'm not trying to be unreasonable, I promise. I just... I can't unsee what's been happening. Am I making any sense?
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or seen things that other people around you didn't seem to notice or couldn't hear or see?

Oh, no. No, nothing like that at all. I mean... I know sometimes people can have those sorts of troubles, and my heart just goes out to them, it really does. But I've never experienced anything like hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there. 

I just... I'm a very practical person, you know? I just go about my day, taking care of the house and trying to be helpful to everybody. My mind is real clear. I wouldn't want you to think I'm losing my marbles or anything like that. I'm just a regular person dealing with a... a difficult family situation. 

I hope that's the right answer? I just want to be as honest and helpful as I can be for you.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a single, fixed, non-bizarre delusional belief (that her husband's sister is manipulating finances to exclude her from decision-making) that has persisted for over a year. The delusion is circumscribed—she denies generalized suspiciousness, mistrust, or paranoia toward others, maintains warm relationships with friends and family, and denies any hallucinations or other psychotic symptoms. She is unable to be dissuaded by contrary evidence, indicating true delusional conviction rather than an overvalued idea. Her affect, behavior, and overall functioning remain otherwise intact, and there is no evidence of thought disorder, negative symptoms, or broader psychotic features that would suggest schizophrenia. This clinical picture—an isolated, non-bizarre delusion with preserved functioning and absence of other psychotic or mood symptoms for greater than one month—is most consistent with Delusional Disorder (F22), persecutory type.
